steps.title: Combining two tables on a shared key
steps.lede: The customers table holds names; the orders table holds delivery times. To see both together, you join them.

blocks.text: QuickCart stores customer names in a customers table and delivery times in a separate orders table. Each orders row carries a customer_id that points back to customers. To see a customer's name alongside their delivery times, you need both tables combined into one result — that's what a JOIN does.

For each row of T1, an INNER JOIN produces a joined row for each row of T2 that satisfies the join condition; rows from either table with no match are dropped. The query SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id pairs every customer row with every order row that shares its customer_id.

The join condition goes in an ON clause — a boolean expression like those used in WHERE — or in a USING clause when both tables share the same column name. ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id can be written USING (customer_id) when the column name is identical in both tables. INNER is the default: writing JOIN alone, without LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL, already means an INNER JOIN.

blocks.title: INNER JOIN: only matched rows survive

Rows with matching customer_id are linked. customer_id=1 (Amara Okafor) matches orders 1001 and 1003; customer_id=2 (Emeka Nwosu) matches order 1002; customer_id=3 (Fatima Aliyu) matches orders 1004 and 1007. customer_id=4 (Chidi Eze) has no matching order and is dropped from the result.

steps.title: INNER JOIN in action
Unmatched rows disappear
steps.lede: An inner join is strict: if one side has no match, that row is gone.

blocks.text: Because it's an inner join, a customer with zero orders — like customer_id 4 (Chidi Eze), who has no row in orders — produces no row at all in the result. Only customers who have at least one matching order appear.

Joining on two columns at once
steps.lede: When a single column isn't enough to uniquely identify a match, you extend ON with AND.

blocks.text: The shipments table records, for each order_id and product_id pair, the date that item actually shipped. Matching shipments to order_items now needs two columns to agree at once — order_id alone isn't enough, because the same order can contain multiple products.

The ON clause takes a boolean expression of the same kind used in WHERE, so several column-equality tests can be combined with AND to require all of them to match before rows join. FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id joins a shipment row only to the order_items row for the exact same order and the exact same product.

USING is a shorthand when both tables share the same column names: USING (a, b) expands to ON T1.a = T2.a AND T1.b = T2.b. Since order_items and shipments both use order_id and product_id, that same join can be written FROM order_items JOIN shipments USING (order_id, product_id).

blocks.code:
-- ON form: two equality tests combined with AND
SELECT oi.order_id, oi.product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  ON oi.order_id = s.order_id
 AND oi.product_id = s.product_id;

-- USING form: shorthand when column names match on both sides
SELECT order_id, product_id, s.shipped_date
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN shipments AS s
  USING (order_id, product_id);

annotations.text: ON with AND: both order_id AND product_id must match
USING: shorthand — expands to the same two-column condition

Keeping unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN
steps.lede: An inner join drops customers with no orders. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, filling missing order columns with NULL.

blocks.text: An inner join between customers and orders drops any customer with zero orders. To list every customer — including those who haven't ordered yet — you need an outer join.

A LEFT OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds a row for each row of T1 with no match in T2, filling T2's columns with NULL. SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id lists every customer; delivery_time_minutes is NULL for any customer with no orders.

blocks.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN
blocks.alt_text: LEFT JOIN: customer_id=1 matches order 1001 normally. Customers 4 and 5 have no orders — they appear in the result with NULL in the delivery_time_minutes column. An INNER JOIN would have dropped them entirely.

steps.title: RIGHT, FULL, and the optional OUTER keyword
steps.lede: LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row. RIGHT and FULL extend that logic to the other side or both sides.

blocks.text: A RIGHT OUTER JOIN is the converse of a left join: it keeps every row of T2, NULL-filling T1's columns for rows of T2 with no match. A FULL OUTER JOIN performs an inner join, then adds NULL-filled rows for the unmatched rows of both T1 and T2 — so no row from either table is lost.
INNER and OUTER are both optional keywords. LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL each already imply an outer join even without writing OUTER, so LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN mean exactly the same thing.

Joins: what you've learned
steps.lede: Three join patterns cover most real-world needs.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides. Extend ON with AND to match on multiple columns, or use USING when the column names are identical. LEFT JOIN keeps every left-side row and NULL-fills the right side for unmatched rows; RIGHT and FULL extend that logic. OUTER is always optional.

blocks.text: SQL clauses are written in one order but processed in another — FROM first, SELECT last. Next you'll trace that order and learn where aliases can and cannot be used.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows survive: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare what an INNER JOIN keeps versus what it drops.

blocks.text: customers has six rows (customer_id 1–6). orders has rows for customer_id 1, 2, and 3 only. An INNER JOIN ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id produces rows only for customers 1, 2, and 3 — the ones with at least one matching order. Customers 4, 5, and 6 have no matching order row, so they are dropped entirely from the result. The rule: a row survives only if both sides have a match.

remediation_steps.title: Extending ON with AND: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: See what changes when you add a second condition to ON.

blocks.text: Single-column join: FROM order_items AS oi JOIN shipments AS s ON oi.order_id = s.order_id — this matches every shipment for the same order, even if the product_id differs. Composite join: ON oi.order_id = s.order_id AND oi.product_id = s.product_id — now both columns must agree. Only the shipment for the exact same order and the exact same product is joined. The ON clause accepts any boolean expression, so AND works the same way it does in WHERE.

remediation_steps.title: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same query with JOIN versus LEFT JOIN gives very different row counts.

blocks.text: INNER JOIN: SELECT c.name, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id — returns only customers 1, 2, and 3, who have orders. Customers 4, 5, and 6 are dropped. LEFT JOIN: replace JOIN with LEFT JOIN — now all six customers appear. Customers 4, 5, and 6 get a row with delivery_time_minutes = NULL. The left table (customers) always contributes at least one row to the result.

tiles.title: Query Execution Order and Subqueries in WHERE

steps.title: SQL clauses run in a different order than you write them
steps.lede: You write SELECT first, but the database processes FROM first. Knowing the real order explains many surprising errors.

blocks.text: A query like SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 0 GROUP BY customer_id HAVING AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30 ORDER BY avg_time DESC is written top to bottom, SELECT first — but that is not the order it is logically processed in.

In a SELECT's general processing order, the FROM list is computed first, then WHERE eliminates non-matching rows, then GROUP BY groups the rows and HAVING eliminates groups, then the SELECT output expressions are computed, and ORDER BY sorts the rows last. In the query above: orders is read, rows with delivery_time_minutes ≤ 0 are dropped, the remaining rows are grouped by customer_id, groups with an average ≤ 30 are removed, the SELECT computes avg_time, and ORDER BY sorts by it.

blocks.title: SQL clause processing order
blocks.alt_text: Six steps left to right: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Each step feeds the next.

steps.title: Tracing the processing order
Where an alias can — and cannot — be used
steps.lede: SELECT runs after WHERE and HAVING, so an alias defined in SELECT isn't visible to those clauses.

blocks.text: An output column's alias, assigned with AS in the SELECT list, can be referred to in ORDER BY and GROUP BY, but not in WHERE or HAVING — those clauses run before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. In the example query, WHERE avg_time > 30 would fail; the expression must be written out in HAVING as AVG(delivery_time_minutes) > 30.

steps.title: Trace the clause processing order

Using a query result as a filter value
steps.lede: When the filter value itself must be computed — like the average delivery time — you embed a query inside WHERE.

blocks.text: Suppose you want the orders that took longer than the average delivery time across all orders. You don't know that average ahead of time — it has to be computed by another query, used right inside the WHERE clause.

A subquery that returns a single (scalar) value can be used as a value expression in a comparison. SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders) keeps only the orders slower than the overall average — the inner SELECT computes that one number, and the outer WHERE compares each row's delivery time against it.

A subquery can also appear as the right side of IN: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40) keeps rows whose customer_id value is found in the subquery's result. SELECT name FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40) finds the customers who have placed at least one order slower than 40 minutes.

blocks.code:
-- Scalar subquery: inner query returns one value
SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes
FROM orders
WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (
    SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes)
    FROM orders
);

-- IN subquery: inner query returns a list of values
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40
);

annotations.text: Inner query: computes one average value
Inner query: returns a list of customer_ids with slow orders

Execution order and WHERE subqueries
steps.lede: Two ideas that explain how SQL really runs.

blocks.text: SQL processes clauses in this order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. An alias defined in SELECT is visible in ORDER BY and GROUP BY, but not in WHERE or HAVING. A subquery in WHERE can return a single value for a comparison or a list of values for IN — the inner query runs first and its result is used by the outer WHERE.

blocks.title: Up next: Subqueries in FROM and CTEs
blocks.text: A subquery can also appear in FROM, acting as a virtual table. CTEs let you name that virtual table once with WITH and reuse it — making complex queries easier to read.

remediation_steps.title: The processing order: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare the written order of clauses with the order they actually run.

blocks.text: Written order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Processing order: FROM (read orders), WHERE (drop rows with delivery_time_minutes ≤ 0), GROUP BY (group by customer_id), HAVING (drop groups with average ≤ 30), SELECT (compute avg_time alias), ORDER BY (sort by avg_time). SELECT runs fifth — not first. That's why an alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE or HAVING.

remediation_steps.title: Scalar subquery in WHERE: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare a hard-coded filter value with one computed by a subquery.

blocks.text: Hard-coded: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 35 — works, but 35 is a guess. Scalar subquery: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > (SELECT AVG(delivery_time_minutes) FROM orders) — the inner query computes the actual average from the data and returns one number; the outer WHERE compares each row against that number. The subquery must return exactly one value to be used in a comparison like > or =.

tiles.title: Subqueries in FROM and Common Table Expressions

steps.title: Treating a query result as a table
steps.lede: Sometimes the thing you want to filter isn't a real table — it's the result of an aggregate query. A subquery in FROM lets you query that result.

blocks.text: Sometimes the thing you want to filter or select from isn't a real table at all, but the result of an aggregate query — like each customer's own average delivery time, treated as if it were a table you could query further.

A subquery used in FROM must be enclosed in parentheses and is typically given a table alias: FROM (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS customer_avg. The SQL standard requires this alias; while PostgreSQL allows it to be omitted, writing one is good practice for portability.

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, avg_time
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id,
           AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) AS customer_avg
WHERE avg_time > 30;

annotations.text: Inner query: computes per-customer average; aliased as customer_avg
Outer query: reads avg_time from the virtual table customer_avg
Outer WHERE: filters using avg_time — the alias the inner query defined

steps.title: Inner column names become the virtual table's columns
steps.lede: The outer query sees the inner query's output columns by their names or aliases.

blocks.text: When a SELECT is used as a subquery, the name of each of its output columns — its own column name or its AS alias — is seen by the outer query as the column name of the virtual table the subquery produces. That's why the outer query can refer to avg_time directly: it's the alias the inner query already gave that column.

Naming a query once with WITH
steps.lede: A CTE lets you define a named result set at the top of a query and read it by name — like a temporary table that exists just for that query.

blocks.text: The customer_avg subquery from before works, but naming it once up front — instead of burying it inside FROM — can make a longer query easier to read.

WITH provides a way to write one or more auxiliary statements — Common Table Expressions (CTEs) — that can be thought of as defining temporary tables that exist just for one query. A CTE is written as WITH name AS (query), and the primary statement then reads it by name, as if it were a table: WITH customer_avg AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30.

A second CTE can read from the first: define customer_avg, then define slow_customers AS (SELECT customer_id FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30), then have the primary query read from slow_customers. Breaking a complex query into named CTEs with WITH is an alternative to nested subqueries, and can make the query easier to follow.

blocks.code:
WITH customer_avg AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
slow_customers AS (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM customer_avg
    WHERE avg_time > 30
)
SELECT c.name, ca.avg_time
FROM customers AS c
JOIN slow_customers AS sc ON c.customer_id = sc.customer_id
JOIN customer_avg AS ca ON c.customer_id = ca.customer_id;

annotations.text: First CTE: customer_avg — per-customer average delivery time
Second CTE: slow_customers — reads from customer_avg
Primary query: reads from both CTEs by name

Subqueries in FROM and CTEs
steps.lede: Two ways to treat a query result as a named table.

blocks.text: A subquery in FROM must be wrapped in parentheses and should be given an alias (the SQL standard requires it, though PostgreSQL allows omission); the outer query reads its output columns by name. A CTE (WITH name AS (query)) names that same idea at the top of the query, making it reusable and easier to read. A second CTE can read from the first; the primary query reads from any CTE by name.

remediation_steps.title: Inner column names: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: See what happens when the outer query uses a column name the inner query didn't define.

blocks.text: Inner query defines: SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id. The virtual table has two columns: customer_id and avg_time. Outer query — correct: SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM (...) AS customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. Outer query — wrong: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 30 — delivery_time_minutes is not a column of the virtual table; the inner query aggregated it away. The outer query can only see the columns the inner query outputs.

remediation_steps.title: Nested subquery vs CTE: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same logic written as a nested subquery and as a CTE.

blocks.text: Nested subquery: SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. CTE equivalent: WITH customer_avg AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(delivery_time_minutes) AS avg_time FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id, avg_time FROM customer_avg WHERE avg_time > 30. Both produce the same result. The CTE names the inner query once at the top; the nested form buries it inside FROM. CTEs are an alternative to nested subqueries and can make the query easier to follow.
